study.title: Come and see the works of God.
study.intro: Twenty verses open with the whole earth shouting, march through the Red Sea and the refining fire of Israel's history, and then narrow to one worshiper who walks into the temple to keep his vows and tell what God did for him.
study.context: The heading names the choirmaster and calls this a song and a psalm, with no author or occasion given. Verses 1–4 summon all the earth to praise. Verses 5–7 invite the nations to 'come and see' the exodus, when God turned the sea into dry land, and perhaps the Jordan crossing too. Verses 8–12 describe Israel's testing: refined like silver, caught in a net, burdened, ridden over, through fire and water, and finally brought into abundance. At verse 13 the voice shifts from 'we' to 'I': one worshiper brings burnt offerings to fulfill vows made in distress. Verses 16–20 become a personal testimony that God heard his prayer.
study.peopleNote: No person is named in the heading. Moses and the exodus generation lie behind verse 6; Moses' profile gives background on the sea crossing. Planned paintings show the sea, fire, silver refining, offerings and anonymous worshipers; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: A joyful noise
verses.heading: All the earth, shout!
verses.meaning: The psalm begins with a shout. 'Make a joyful noise' translates a word for the loud cry raised at a king's coronation or on a battlefield after victory. It is not refined music but full-throated acclaim. And it is addressed to 'all the earth', not just Israel. From the very first line, this psalm insists that the God of Israel deserves praise from every nation. What He has done for one people is meant to make the whole world cheer.
verses.context: Psalm 100:1 uses the same summons. 1 Samuel 10:24 records the people shouting 'Long live the king!' at Saul's coronation, a similar acclaim. Revelation 7:9–10 shows every nation crying out praise to God.
explore: Joyful noise
A ringing shout of acclaim, the kind raised for a victorious king.
All the earth
Every land and people. Israel's praise is meant to become the world's praise.
verses.reflect: When did you last praise God loudly and freely, without worrying how it sounded?
verses.alt: Crowds on a broad hillside raise their arms in celebration under a vast sky.

verses.title: Glorious praise
verses.heading: Singing the honor of His name
verses.meaning: The shout becomes a song. 'Sing the glory of His name' means to celebrate the honor and weight of who God has revealed Himself to be. 'Make His praise glorious' asks for worship that fits its object. If God is glorious, praise should not be careless or half-hearted. This is not about musical perfection but about giving God the honor He is due, with hearts and voices that take Him seriously.
verses.context: Psalm 29:2 says 'Ascribe to the LORD the glory due His name.' 1 Chronicles 16:29 repeats it at the ark's arrival in Jerusalem, and Revelation 4:11 declares God worthy to receive glory and honor.
explore: Glory of His name
The splendor and honor of God's revealed character, summed up in His name.
Make His praise glorious
Let worship match the greatness of the One being praised.
verses.reflect: What would it look like to make your worship match how great God really is?
verses.alt: Musicians with lyres and tambourines play on wide stone steps in golden light.

verses.title: How awesome!
verses.heading: Enemies cower
verses.meaning: The psalm gives the worshipers words to say directly to God: 'How awesome are Your deeds!' Awesome here means fearsome, deeds that make people tremble. God's power is so great that His enemies 'cower', a word that suggests cringing or feigned submission. Those who oppose Him cannot stand in the open against Him. Their bowing may be forced, but it shows that no rebel power can outlast the God whose deeds shook Egypt and parted the sea.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 33:29 says Israel's enemies will cower before them. Exodus 15:14–16 describes the nations trembling as they hear of the sea crossing, and Philippians 2:10 says every knee will bow.
explore: Awesome
Inspiring fear and wonder. God's acts make people stop and tremble.
Cower
To cringe or pretend submission. Enemies bow, whether they want to or not.
verses.reflect: Which of God's deeds in Scripture or in your life most fills you with awe?
verses.alt: A line of chariots halts at a riverbank, horses rearing before rising water.

verses.title: All the earth bows
verses.heading: A world singing His name
verses.meaning: The words the worshipers speak to God continue: all the earth bows down to You. What began as a command in verse 1 is now pictured as reality. The nations not only bow but sing, and they sing praise 'to Your name'. Bowing alone could be fearful submission; singing shows joyful allegiance. The psalm looks forward to a day when the whole world worships the God of Israel gladly. 'Selah' invites the listener to pause and imagine that scene.
verses.context: Psalm 22:27 promises that all the ends of the earth will turn to the LORD. Zechariah 14:9 says the LORD will be king over all the earth, and Revelation 15:4 asks, 'Who will not fear You, O Lord?'
explore: Bows down
Kneeling or bowing low, a posture of worship and submission.
Sing praise to Your name
Joyful, willing worship of God's revealed character, not just forced submission.
verses.reflect: How do you picture the day when all the earth worships God? What part might you play in it now?
verses.alt: People from many lands kneel together on a broad plain at sunrise.

verses.title: Come and see
verses.heading: An invitation to look
verses.meaning: 'Come and see' is one of the great invitations of Scripture. The psalmist does not argue for God; he points. Look at what God has done toward mankind. His deeds are not hidden in theory but displayed in history, in real events that can be told and examined. The phrase 'toward mankind' shows that God's mighty acts are not cold displays of power. They are directed toward people, for their good. This is the psalm's cover verse, the hinge between the global shout and Israel's story.
verses.context: In John 1:39 and 1:46 Jesus and Philip use the same invitation, 'Come and see'. Psalm 46:8 says 'Come, see the works of the LORD.' Faith in the Bible rests on what God has done.
explore: Works of God
God's acts in history, such as creation, the exodus and rescues of His people.
Toward mankind
God's deeds are aimed at people, showing His care as well as His power.
verses.reflect: If someone asked why you believe, what work of God could you invite them to 'come and see'?
verses.alt: A villager points from a cliff edge toward a wide sea gleaming far below.

verses.title: Through the waters on foot
verses.heading: There we rejoiced
verses.meaning: The psalm reaches for Israel's founding miracle. God 'turned the sea into dry land', the Red Sea crossing of Exodus 14. 'They passed through the waters on foot' may also recall the Jordan, when the river stopped for Joshua's generation. Then the pronoun changes: 'there we rejoiced in Him.' Though centuries have passed, the worshipers claim the story as their own. Remembering in Israel was not just recalling facts. It was standing inside the story as if you had been there.
verses.context: Exodus 14:21–22 describes the sea parting and Israel walking through on dry ground. Joshua 3:16–17 shows the Jordan stopping for Israel to cross. Exodus 15:1–21 records Moses' and Miriam's songs on the far shore.
explore: Sea into dry land
The Red Sea crossing, the central rescue of Israel's history.
There we rejoiced
Later generations join the celebration as though they had stood on the shore themselves.
verses.reflect: What story of God's rescue, from Scripture or your family, do you claim as your own?
verses.alt: A dry path runs between towering walls of blue-green water under a dawn sky.

verses.title: His eyes watch
verses.heading: A warning to rebels
verses.meaning: The God who split the sea still reigns. 'He rules forever by His power' moves from past rescue to present rule. 'His eyes watch the nations' means nothing escapes His notice; He keeps watch like a sentry over the world's affairs. That leads to a warning: 'Do not let the rebellious exalt themselves.' Pharaoh had exalted himself against God and ended in the sea. Any nation or person who rises in pride against the LORD should remember how that story ended.
verses.context: Exodus 5:2 records Pharaoh asking, 'Who is the LORD that I should obey Him?' Proverbs 16:18 warns that pride goes before destruction. 2 Chronicles 16:9 says the LORD's eyes roam the whole earth.
explore: Rules forever
God's reign did not end with the exodus. He still governs history.
Rebellious
Those who stubbornly resist God. They are warned not to lift themselves up in pride.
verses.reflect: Where might pride be rising in you against God's ways? How does this warning speak to you?
verses.alt: A tall watchtower overlooks a crossroads where caravans meet at dusk.

verses.title: Bless our God
verses.heading: Let the sound be heard
verses.meaning: The call to praise goes out again to the 'peoples', the nations of the earth. This time it is not 'come and see' but 'bless our God'. To bless God is to speak well of Him, to honor Him for who He is and what He has done. 'Let the sound of His praise be heard' asks for praise that is audible and public, not just private gratitude. Israel's testimony was meant to ring out so that other nations would hear and join the song.
verses.context: Psalm 96:3 says, 'Declare His glory among the nations.' Romans 15:11 quotes Psalm 117:1, 'Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles', as part of God's plan for the nations.
explore: Bless
To praise and speak well of. When people bless God, they honor His goodness.
Be heard
Praise is meant to be public and audible, a witness to others.
verses.reflect: How could your praise for God be heard by someone else this week?
verses.alt: A shepherd plays a reed flute on a hilltop as villagers stop in the fields below.

verses.title: Feet from slipping
verses.heading: Kept alive
verses.meaning: Before describing hardship, the psalm states the bottom line: God 'preserves our lives', literally sets our soul among the living. He 'keeps our feet from slipping'. On rocky hill paths a slip could be fatal, so the image speaks of God's steadying care through dangerous terrain. The trials of verses 10–12 were real and painful, but they were never the whole story. Through all of them God kept His people alive and on their feet.
verses.context: Psalm 121:3 says, 'He will not allow your foot to slip.' 1 Samuel 2:9 says God guards the feet of His faithful ones, and Jude 24 praises the One who is able to keep you from stumbling.
explore: Preserves our lives
Keeps us among the living. God sustained Israel through every danger.
Feet from slipping
An image of steady footing on treacherous paths, a picture of daily protection.
verses.reflect: Where has God kept your feet from slipping when the path was steep?
verses.alt: A walker's sandals find firm footing on a narrow mountain trail above a gorge.

verses.title: Refined like silver
verses.heading: The purpose of testing
verses.meaning: Now the psalm explains Israel's hard seasons. 'You, O God, have tested us' names God as the one behind the testing, not to destroy but to prove. 'You have refined us like silver' describes the work of a silversmith who melts the ore in a crucible so the impurities rise and can be skimmed off. The fire is hot, but it is purposeful. The goal is pure silver that reflects the refiner's face. Hardship in God's hands is not random; it is refining.
verses.context: Malachi 3:3 pictures the LORD as a refiner purifying the Levites like silver. Isaiah 48:10 says, 'I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tested you in the furnace of affliction.' 1 Peter 1:7 says faith is refined by fire.
explore: Tested
Proved or examined, as metal is tried, to reveal what is genuine.
Refined
Purified by heat. Silver was melted so its dross could be removed.
verses.reflect: What hardship might God be using to refine something in you rather than to punish you?
verses.alt: Molten silver glows in a clay crucible over coals in a small workshop.

verses.title: Net and burdens
verses.heading: Trapped and weighed down
verses.meaning: The testing included seasons of entrapment and heavy loads. 'You led us into the net' pictures Israel like a bird or animal caught in a hunter's trap, perhaps in times of siege or captivity. 'You laid burdens on our backs' recalls forced labor, like the bricks of Egypt or the tribute of foreign kings. The psalm says plainly that God allowed these hardships. This is not a cold claim but an honest confession that even dark seasons are held within God's purposes.
verses.context: Exodus 1:11–14 describes Israel's crushing labor in Egypt. Lamentations 1:13–14 speaks of a net spread for the feet and a yoke of sins bound on the neck. Matthew 11:28–30 offers a lighter burden.
explore: Net
A hunter's trap. It pictures being caught, restricted and helpless.
Burdens on our backs
Heavy loads, like the forced labor of slaves in Egypt.
verses.reflect: What net or burden feels heaviest in your life? How does it help to bring it honestly to God?
verses.alt: A heavy bundle of mud bricks sits on the ground beside a rope net in harsh light.

verses.title: Into abundance
verses.heading: Through fire and water
verses.meaning: The hardship reaches its worst: 'You let men ride over our heads', a picture of enemies trampling a defeated people like chariots over fallen soldiers. 'We went through fire and water' sums up every kind of danger. But then comes the turn: 'You brought us into abundance.' The word means a place of overflow, a full cup. The trials were real, but they were a passage, not a destination. God led His people through the fire and water and out the other side.
verses.context: Isaiah 43:2 promises, 'When you pass through the waters, I will be with you... when you walk through the fire, you will not be burned.' Psalm 23:5 says 'my cup overflows'. Daniel 3:25–27 shows three men walking unharmed in fire.
explore: Ride over our heads
Enemies trampling or riding over a conquered people, an image of humiliation.
Abundance
A place of overflowing plenty, like a cup filled to running over.
verses.reflect: What fire or water are you passing through? What might the abundance on the other side look like?
verses.alt: A path leads out of a smoky ravine into a broad green valley full of orchards.

verses.title: Entering Your house
verses.heading: Keeping vows
verses.meaning: Here the psalm narrows from 'we' to 'I'. One worshiper steps forward and walks into God's house with burnt offerings. A burnt offering was wholly given to God, burned completely on the altar, a sign of total dedication. He comes to 'fulfill my vows', promises made when he needed help. National history has become personal worship. The story of a whole people's rescue flows into one person's thanksgiving, as if he has gone through his own fire and water.
verses.context: Leviticus 1 describes the burnt offering, entirely consumed on the altar. Psalm 116:12–14 asks 'How can I repay the LORD?' and answers by fulfilling vows in the presence of His people.
explore: Burnt offerings
Sacrifices wholly burned on the altar, expressing total devotion to God.
Fulfill my vows
Keeping promises made to God during trouble, now that He has answered.
verses.reflect: What would it look like for you to offer something wholly to God in thanks for what He has done?
verses.alt: A worshiper leads a young ram through a stone gateway into a sunlit courtyard.

verses.title: Promised in distress
verses.heading: Words spoken under pressure
verses.meaning: The vows he is keeping were made 'in my distress'. In the moment of crisis, he opened his mouth and promised God thanks if He would rescue him. Many people make such promises and forget them once the danger passes. This worshiper remembers. 'My lips promised and my mouth spoke' stresses that the words were real, spoken aloud, not vague intentions. Integrity before God means honoring words spoken in desperation as seriously as words spoken in calm.
verses.context: Jonah 2:9 records Jonah in the fish promising, 'What I have vowed I will make good.' Ecclesiastes 5:4–5 warns that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. Hannah keeps her vow to give Samuel in 1 Samuel 1:27–28.
explore: My lips promised
Words actually spoken aloud, committing the speaker before God.
In my distress
Under pressure, in a tight place. Promises made there are still binding.
verses.reflect: Have you ever promised God something in a crisis? Is there anything left to fulfill?
verses.alt: A small clay lamp burns beside an open scroll on a low table in dim light.

verses.title: Fragrant smoke
verses.heading: Lavish thanksgiving
verses.meaning: The offering he describes is generous: fatlings, rams, bulls and goats. These were valuable animals, the best of a herd. 'Fragrant smoke of rams' pictures the smoke rising from the altar, a sweet aroma ascending to God. The list seems almost extravagant, which is the point. Gratitude that matches the rescue does not count the cost. The 'Selah' invites us to pause and consider what a lavish response to God's goodness might look like in our own lives.
verses.context: David refused to offer God what cost him nothing in 2 Samuel 24:24. Genesis 8:20–21 says the LORD smelled the pleasing aroma of Noah's offering, and Ephesians 5:2 calls Christ's sacrifice a fragrant offering.
explore: Fatlings
The best-fed animals, the most valuable in a flock or herd.
Fragrant smoke
The aroma rising from the altar, pictured as pleasing to God.
verses.reflect: What would a generous, not-counting-the-cost response to God look like for you this week?
verses.alt: Smoke curls upward from a stone altar into a clear blue morning sky.

verses.title: Come and listen
verses.heading: A personal testimony
verses.meaning: The call 'come and see' in verse 5 now becomes 'come and listen'. The nations were invited to see God's works in history; now God's people are invited to hear what He has done for one person. 'All you who fear God' are those who revere Him and will understand. Personal testimony stands beside national history. The grand story of the sea crossing and the small story of one answered prayer are both worth telling.
verses.context: Psalm 34:11 invites, 'Come, children, listen to me.' Mark 5:19 records Jesus telling a healed man to go home and tell what the Lord had done for him. 1 Peter 3:15 urges readiness to give a reason for hope.
explore: Come and listen
An invitation to hear a personal account of God's faithfulness.
What He has done for me
Testimony rooted in personal experience, not only in history.
verses.reflect: What has God done for you personally that someone else might need to hear?
verses.alt: An old woman speaks to a circle of listeners gathered on a doorstep at evening.

verses.title: Praise on the tongue
verses.heading: Crying out and praising together
verses.meaning: His testimony begins simply: 'I cried out to Him with my mouth.' He prayed aloud in his trouble. Then, 'praised Him with my tongue', or as some read it, praise was already under his tongue, ready to come out. Even while asking for help, he was already praising. Cry and praise were not separated in time. Faith often looks like this: the request and the thanksgiving rising together, because the one praying trusts that God will hear.
verses.context: Philippians 4:6 urges prayer 'with thanksgiving'. Jonah 2:9 combines a cry from the depths with a song of thanks, and Acts 16:25 shows Paul and Silas singing hymns in prison.
explore: Cried out
Called aloud for help in a time of real need and danger.
Praised Him with my tongue
Praise ready on his lips, even before the answer came.
verses.reflect: Can you add thanksgiving to a prayer you are still waiting to see answered?
verses.alt: A figure sits in a prison cell singing, with moonlight falling through a high slit.

verses.title: Cherished iniquity
verses.heading: An honest heart
verses.meaning: The worshiper pauses to make a sober point. 'If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened.' To cherish iniquity is to look on sin with approval, to hold it dear and refuse to let it go. That is different from struggling with sin or confessing it. Prayer is not a magic formula that works whatever the heart is doing. God listens to the humble and repentant, not to those who want His help while clinging to what He hates.
verses.context: Isaiah 59:2 says iniquities have made a separation between people and God. Proverbs 28:9 warns that the prayer of one who turns from the law is detestable. James 5:16 says the prayer of a righteous person is powerful.
explore: Cherished
Regarded with favor, held on to. It describes sin welcomed rather than resisted.
Would not have listened
Not a denial of grace, but a warning that unrepentant sin blocks honest prayer.
verses.reflect: Is there any sin you are holding on to that could be blocking your prayers? What would letting go look like?
verses.alt: A hand opens to release a small dark stone into a flowing clear stream.

verses.title: Surely heard
verses.heading: The answer came
verses.meaning: 'But God has surely heard.' The word 'surely' expresses certainty and relief. The speaker had not cherished sin; he had come honestly, and God listened. 'He has attended to the sound of my prayer' uses a word for paying close attention, leaning in to catch every word. This is the heart of his testimony. Not the burnt offerings, not his own goodness, but this: God heard him. That one fact is what he wants everyone who fears God to know.
verses.context: Psalm 6:9 says, 'The LORD has heard my cry for mercy.' Exodus 3:7 records God saying He has heard the cry of His people in Egypt. 1 John 5:14–15 says that if we ask according to His will, He hears us.
explore: Surely
Truly, certainly. The speaker has no doubt that God has answered.
Attended
Listened carefully, paid close attention to every word of the prayer.
verses.reflect: When have you known for certain that God heard you? How does that memory strengthen you now?
verses.alt: Morning sunlight pours through a window onto a woman kneeling with her face lifted.

verses.title: Not rejected
verses.heading: Love not withheld
verses.meaning: The psalm ends with a blessing on God that sums up everything. He 'has not rejected my prayer', He did not push it away or ignore it. And He has not 'withheld from me His loving devotion'. The final word, hesed, God's covenant love, is the deepest reason for praise. Answered prayer is wonderful, but the deeper gift is that God's steadfast love was never taken away. The worshiper who walked through fire and water ends by blessing a God who never stopped loving him.
verses.context: Lamentations 3:22 says the LORD's loving devotion never ceases. Romans 8:35–39 asks what can separate us from the love of Christ and answers: nothing. Psalm 136 repeats 'His loving devotion endures forever'.
explore: Not rejected
God did not turn away, push aside or dismiss the prayer.
Loving devotion
Hesed, God's loyal covenant love. It was never withheld, even in the testing.
verses.reflect: How does knowing that God's love has never been withheld from you change how you pray?
verses.alt: A wide sunrise lights a valley where a road climbs toward a distant hill city.
